```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# the package load must sit in this unconditional chunk: the tangled
# script skips eval-gated chunks, so a library() inside one leaves
# every later unconditional chunk without frm()
library(frmtmb)
has_lme4 <- requireNamespace("lme4", quietly = TRUE)
has_tinyplot <- requireNamespace("tinyplot", quietly = TRUE)
```

frmtmb fits regression models written in the brms formula grammar by
maximum likelihood, with the Laplace approximation for random effects.
The backend is RTMB: the model formula compiles to an R objective
function that is differentiated on the TMB AD tape. There is no MCMC and
no compilation at run time.

## A mixed model

```{r, eval = has_lme4}
data(sleepstudy, package = "lme4")

fit <- frm(bf(Reaction ~ Days + (Days | Subject)), family = gaussian(),
           data = sleepstudy)
summary(fit)
```

The usual methods work: `fixef()`, `ranef()`, `VarCorr()`, `fitted()`
and `predict()` (brms's summary matrices, the second with observation
noise in it), `frm_linpred()` (the linear predictor, with `newdata`,
`se.fit` and `re_formula`), `confint()` (Wald, profile, or
likelihood-root), `simulate()`, `anova()` for likelihood-ratio tests,
and `emmeans` for marginal means.

`fitted()` gives the fit its own picture. One panel per subject shows
what the random slopes bought: the lines share a population trend, but
each subject keeps its own intercept and its own slope.

```{r sleep-fig, eval = has_lme4 && has_tinyplot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Eighteen small panels, one for each subject of the sleep deprivation study. Gray points are the observed reaction times against days of sleep deprivation. A red line in each panel is the fitted value for that subject. Most lines rise, and their slopes differ from panel to panel. One subject has a flat line."}
sleepstudy$yhat <- fitted(fit)[, "Estimate"]
tinyplot::tinyplot(Reaction ~ Days, data = sleepstudy, facet = ~Subject,
                   type = "p", pch = 16, cex = 0.7, col = "gray40",
                   theme = "clean2", facet.args = list(nrow = 3))
tinyplot::plt_add(yhat ~ Days, data = sleepstudy, facet = ~Subject,
                  type = "l", col = "firebrick", lwd = 1.5)
```

The figures on this page use
[tinyplot](https://cran.r-project.org/package=tinyplot), which is a
suggested package. They are skipped when it is not installed.

## Distributional regression

Every distributional parameter can get its own formula with the full
predictor grammar, including random effects and smooths:

```{r, eval = has_lme4}
fit2 <- frm(bf(Reaction ~ Days + (Days | Subject),
               sigma ~ Days), family = gaussian(),
            data = sleepstudy)
fixef_by_dpar(fit2)$sigma
```

The coefficient on `Days` is positive, so the model says that reaction
times scatter more widely late in the study. Compare the fitted
residual standard deviation with the standard deviation of the
residuals on each day.

```{r sigma-fig, eval = has_lme4 && has_tinyplot, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Scatter plot of residual standard deviation against days of sleep deprivation. Ten gray points are the observed standard deviations, one for each day. A red curve is the fitted residual standard deviation. Both rise from about 17 on day zero to about 36 on day nine."}
day_sd <- as.numeric(tapply(residuals(fit2)[, "Estimate"],
                            sleepstudy$Days, sd))
sig <- as.numeric(frm_linpred(fit2, dpar = "sigma", type = "response",
                          newdata = data.frame(Days = 0:9,
                                               Subject = "308")))
tinyplot::tinyplot(x = 0:9, y = day_sd, type = "p", pch = 16,
                   col = "gray30", theme = "clean2", xlab = "Days",
                   ylab = "residual standard deviation",
                   ylim = range(c(day_sd, sig)))
tinyplot::plt_add(x = 0:9, y = sig, type = "l", col = "firebrick",
                  lwd = 2)
```

The daily standard deviations are noisy, because each one comes from 18
observations. The trend they show is the trend the model fits.

## Nonlinear formulas

With `nl = TRUE` the model formula is an arbitrary R expression over
named parameters, each of which has its own linear predictor:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(x = runif(200, 0, 5))
d$y <- 2.5 * exp(-0.7 * d$x) + rnorm(200, 0, 0.15)
nlfit <- frm(bf(y ~ a * exp(-b * x), a ~ 1, b ~ 1, nl = TRUE) +
               gaussian(),
             data = d, start = list(beta = c(1, 0.3)))
fixef(nlfit, flatten = TRUE)
```

Every nonlinear parameter starts at zero unless `start` or a located
prior moves it. For a monotone term that is usually good enough. For a
BUMP-SHAPED term it is not, because a bump evaluated away from the data
is flat in every one of its parameters at once. Write a peak
`exp(lamp) * exp(-0.5 * ((w - pk) / exp(lsig))^2)` over `w` from 1 to
45 and `pk` starts at 0, where the bump underflows to zero everywhere:
the amplitude, the centre and the width then have no gradient, the
Hessian is singular and every standard error is `NaN`. The fit is not
overparameterized. It never had a gradient to follow.

Two spellings avoid it. Put the centre where the data is, either with a
start value or by writing the offset into the formula:

```r
# start the centre in the middle of the range
frm(bf(I ~ exp(lamp) * exp(-0.5 * ((w - pk) / exp(lsig))^2),
       pk ~ 1, lamp ~ 1, lsig ~ 1, nl = TRUE),
    family = exponential("log"), data = d,
    start = list(beta = c("pk_(Intercept)" = 10)))

# or estimate a DEPARTURE from a centre you already know
bf(I ~ exp(lamp) * exp(-0.5 * ((w - (10 + pk)) / exp(lsig))^2), ...)
```

`diagnose(fit)` names the flat parameters when this happens, under
"Flat directions".

A nonlinear parameter also cannot be named after one of the family's
own distributional parameters. `mu ~ 1 + (1 | id)` in a `nl = TRUE`
model gives the family's own `mu` a linear predictor, and the model
body then has no `mu` to refer to; `frm()` refuses it and names the
reserved set. Any other name is free, including `b` and `theta`. Those
two are also parameter-template component names, so `start = list(b =
)` still means the random-effect vector, not the parameter: a
nonlinear parameter's coefficients live inside `beta`, as
`start = list(beta = c("b_(Intercept)" = 1))`.

## Custom families

A family is a plain R function returning an AD-safe log-density; no
Stan or C++ involved:

```{r}
my_poisson <- custom_family(
  "my_poisson", dpars = "mu", links = list(mu = "log"),
  lpdf = function(y, dpars, aterms) {
    y * log(dpars$mu) - dpars$mu - lgamma(y + 1)
  }
)
check_custom_family(my_poisson, y = rpois(50, 3),
                    dpars = list(mu = rep(2.5, 50)))
```

An inverse link saturates, so a density written over `1 - mu` or
`log(mu)` loses the tail: `plogis(eta)` is exactly 1 in double precision
from `eta = 36.7368` up, and there `1 - mu` is exactly 0, which gives
`NaN` for the value and for the gradient. `frm()` keeps each linear
predictor beside its distributional parameter while the objective is
taped, and `?"frmtmb-robust-dpars"` is how a density reads it.

```{r}
# a gate the optimizer has pushed against 1
d_on <- list(zi = plogis(40), .eta_zi = 40)
c(plain = log(1 - d_on$zi),
  robust = dpar_log1m(d_on, "zi", "logit"))
```

`check_custom_family()` supplies no linear predictors, so it exercises
the fallback path only. Test the other one by building the `dpars` list
by hand, as above.

## Smooths and Gaussian processes

mgcv smooths and `gp()` terms work in any linear predictor; their
smoothing and kernel parameters are estimated as variance components.
`gp()` takes up to three variables and brms's arguments: `iso = TRUE`,
the default, shares one lengthscale and `iso = FALSE` gives one per
dimension, and `by = f` fits one GP per level of a factor, with its
own standard deviation and lengthscale, or multiplies the GP by a
numeric `by`. The exact form predicts at new
positions by kriging; the Hilbert-space form (`k =`) interpolates
through its basis, capped at `k^D <= 1000` columns. The Hilbert-space
form uses brms's input convention: the coordinates are divided by their
largest pairwise distance, so the boundary factor `c =` (1.25 by
default, one value per variable) means the same thing here as in brms.
Reported lengthscales stay in data units.

```{r}
set.seed(2)
ds <- data.frame(x = runif(200, 0, 10))
ds$y <- sin(ds$x) + rnorm(200, 0, 0.4)
fs <- frm(bf(y ~ s(x)), family = gaussian(), data = ds)
fg <- frm(bf(y ~ gp(x, k = 25)), family = gaussian(), data = ds)
c(smooth = AIC(fs), gp = AIC(fg))
```

## Spatial Gaussian Markov random fields

`car()`, brms's conditional autoregressive field over an adjacency
matrix, and `spde()`, a Matern field over a finite-element mesh, are in
the extension package frmtmb.spatial. Load it with
`library(frmtmb.spatial)`; its vignette,
`vignette("spatial", package = "frmtmb.spatial")`, covers both. Without
the package, `frm()` refuses either term by name and says how to load
it.

## Special terms

`mo()` fits monotonic effects of ordinal predictors, `mi()` imputes
missing continuous predictors inside the model (with `mi(sdx)` for
known measurement error), and `se()` gives meta-analysis:

```{r}
set.seed(3)
dm <- data.frame(inc = sample(0:3, 300, TRUE), z = rnorm(300))
dm$y <- 1 + c(0, 1, 1.6, 2)[dm$inc + 1] + 0.3 * dm$z + rnorm(300)
fmo <- frm(bf(y ~ mo(inc) + z), family = gaussian(), data = dm)
frm_linpred(fmo, newdata = data.frame(inc = 0:3, z = 0))
```

## Mixtures

Finite mixtures keep per-component parameters and covariate-dependent
mixing weights; `groups = ~g` moves the class draw to the group level
(latent classes, combinable with random effects):

```{r}
mix <- mixture(gaussian(), gaussian(), groups = ~g)
dmix <- data.frame(y = 0, g = factor(rep(1:40, each = 5)))
# frm_simulate() draws one class per GROUP here, which is what
# groups = ~g means; theta1 and theta2 are the mixing probabilities,
# brms's simplex, set together
dmix$y <- frm_simulate(bf(y ~ 1) + mix, dmix,
                       newparams = list(b_mu1_Intercept = -1,
                                        b_mu2_Intercept = 2,
                                        sigma1 = 0.8, sigma2 = 0.8,
                                        theta1 = 0.6, theta2 = 0.4),
                       nsim = 1, seed = 4)[[1]]
fmix <- frm(bf(y ~ 1) + mix, data = dmix)
head(mixture_probs(fmix), 3)
```

## Inference beyond Wald

`hypothesis()` tests arbitrary parameter expressions (Wald, profile,
or parametric bootstrap) and returns brms's object. It uses brms's
names: `b_Days` for a coefficient, which brms's default `class = "b"`
lets you write `Days`, and natural-scale names such as
`sd_Subject__Days`, which need `class = NULL`:

```{r, eval = has_lme4}
hypothesis(fit, "Days > 5")
hypothesis(fit, "sd_Subject__Days^2 / (sd_Subject__Days^2 + sigma^2) = 0",
           class = NULL)
```

`frm_bootstrap()` runs a warm-started parametric bootstrap, and
`confint(fit, method = "profile")` profiles single parameters.

## Simulating from a design

`frm_simulate()` builds a design from a formula and data, sets the
parameters, and simulates responses - no fit needed. This is the power
analysis loop: simulate, refit, count. Parameters take brms's names,
the strings `variables()` returns: `b_x` for a coefficient, on the link
scale; `sigma` as a residual SD; and `sd_<group>__<term>` as a standard
deviation. A bare name such as `x` is refused with its brms spelling:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
dd <- data.frame(x = rnorm(120), g = factor(rep(1:12, 10)), y = 0)
form <- bf(y ~ x + (1 | g)) + gaussian()
# The draw takes its own seed, away from the chunk's: reusing
# set.seed(1) restarts the same random stream that made x, and the
# residuals come out equal to the covariate.
sims <- frm_simulate(form, dd, nsim = 3, seed = 1001,
                     newparams = list(b_Intercept = 1, b_x = 0.5,
                                      sigma = 0.6,
                                      sd_g__Intercept = 0.7))
str(sims, max.level = 0)
```

Give `prior` instead and every simulation draws its own parameter
vector first - the analog of brms's `sample_prior = "only"` followed by
`posterior_predict()`. The drawn parameters come back as an attribute,
so a prior-predictive check can relate parameters to outcomes:

```{r prior-pred, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Scatter plot of the standard deviation of each simulated response set against the slope that generated it. The points form a U shape, because a larger slope of either sign spreads the outcome more."}
pp <- frm_simulate(form, dd, nsim = 50, seed = 2,
                   prior = set_prior("normal(0, 1)", class = "b") +
                     set_prior("normal(0, 2)", class = "Intercept") +
                     set_prior("exponential(1)", class = "sd") +
                     set_prior("exponential(1)", class = "sigma"))
pars <- attr(pp, "pars")
head(pars, 3)
# does the prior imply plausible data? slope against outcome spread
plot(pars$b_x, apply(pp, 2, sd), xlab = "slope", ylab = "sd(y)")
```

Every coefficient and every random-effect SD needs a value from
`newparams` or a prior; leaving one out is an error rather than a
silent zero effect.

## Diagnostics

`diagnose(fit)` reports convergence forensics. Simulation-based
residuals come through DHARMa, predictive checks through
`pp_check()`, and effect displays through `conditional_effects()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
plot(dharma_residuals(fit))
plot(conditional_effects(fit))
```

The same fitted objective can be handed to NUTS for full Bayes on the
same model. That lives in the companion package **frmtmb.sample**:
`frmtmb.sample::frm_sample()` returns draws with the whole posterior
method surface (`posterior_epred()`, `hypothesis()`, `loo()`), and
`frmtmb.sample::check_laplace()` audits the Laplace approximation
against them.

See `vignette("inputs")` for what `frm()` accepts and what it costs to
run, `vignette("brms-migration")` for the brms feature map, and
`vignette("diagnostics")` for the model-checking workflow.
